{"problem": {"theorem": "Prove that any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "abstract_algebra", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "candidates": [{"candidate_id": "choice-1", "text": "Let G and H be nonabelian groups of order 21. By Sylow’s theorems, the number of Sylow 7-subgroups divides 3 and is congruent to 1 modulo 7, so each group has a unique, hence normal, Sylow 7-subgroup. Write P=⟨b⟩ in G and R=⟨d⟩ in H, where b and d have order 7. Choose elements a∈G and c∈H of order 3.

Since ⟨a⟩∩P={e} and |⟨a⟩||P|=21, every element of G has a unique form b^s a^r, with s modulo 7 and r modulo 3. Similarly, every element of H has a unique form d^s c^r.

Because P is normal, conjugation by a induces an automorphism of P, so

a b a^{-1}=b^i

for some i∈{1,2,3,4,5,6}. Since a^3=e, conjugating three times gives b=b^{i^3}, hence i^3≡1 (mod 7). The solutions are i∈{1,2,4}. If i=1, then a and b commute; as they generate G, this would make G abelian. Thus i∈{2,4}. Likewise,

c d c^{-1}=d^j

for some j∈{2,4}.

Choose x∈H as follows: if i=j, let x=c; if i≠j, let x=c^{-1}. Since 2 and 4 are inverses modulo 7, in either case x has order 3 and

x d x^{-1}=d^i.

Also ⟨x⟩=⟨c⟩, so every element of H has a unique form d^s x^r. Define

φ:G→H, φ(b^s a^r)=d^s x^r.

This is well-defined and bijective by uniqueness of the two normal forms. Moreover, from a^r b^t a^{-r}=b^{i^r t},

(b^s a^r)(b^t a^u)=b^{s+i^r t}a^{r+u},

where exponents are reduced modulo 7 and 3. The identical formula holds in H because x^r d^t x^{-r}=d^{i^r t}. Therefore

φ((b^s a^r)(b^t a^u))=φ(b^s a^r)φ(b^t a^u),

so φ is a bijective homomorphism. Hence G≅H. Therefore any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic."}, {"candidate_id": "choice-2", "text": "Let G and H be arbitrary nonabelian groups of order 21.

By Sylow’s theorems, the number of Sylow 7-subgroups of G divides 3 and is congruent to 1 modulo 7, so G has a unique, hence normal, Sylow 7-subgroup N=⟨b⟩. Let A=⟨a⟩ be a Sylow 3-subgroup. Since N∩A={e}, we have |NA|=7·3=21, so G=NA. Thus every element of G has a unique expression b^j a^k, with j modulo 7 and k modulo 3.

Conjugation by a is an automorphism of N, so

a b a^{-1}=b^r

for some r∈{1,…,6}. Since a^3=e,

b=a^3ba^{-3}=b^{r^3},

and hence r^3≡1 (mod 7). The solutions are r≡1,2,4 (mod 7). If r=1, then a and b commute; because they generate G, this would make G abelian. Therefore r∈{2,4}.

Apply the same argument to H. Choose generators c and d of Sylow subgroups of orders 3 and 7, respectively, so that

c d c^{-1}=d^s,

where s∈{2,4}. Define x=c if s=r, and x=c^{-1} if s≠r. In the latter case, s^{-1}≡r (mod 7), since 2 and 4 are inverses modulo 7. Consequently, in both cases,

x d x^{-1}=d^r.

Define φ:G→H using the unique normal forms by

φ(b^j a^k)=d^j x^k.

In G the relation aba^{-1}=b^r gives

(b^j a^k)(b^ℓ a^m)=b^{j+r^kℓ}a^{k+m}.

The identical formula holds in H with d and x. Therefore

φ((b^j a^k)(b^ℓ a^m))=φ(b^j a^k)φ(b^ℓ a^m),

so φ is a homomorphism. Every element of H has a unique form d^j x^k, hence φ is bijective. Thus G≅H. Since G and H were arbitrary, any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic."}, {"candidate_id": "choice-3", "text": "Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be arbitrary nonabelian groups of order \(21\). We show that both have the same normal-form multiplication.

By Sylow's theorems, the number \(n_7\) of Sylow \(7\)-subgroups satisfies \(n_7\mid 3\) and \(n_7\equiv1\pmod 7\), so \(n_7=1\). Thus \(G\) has a normal cyclic subgroup \(N=\langle b\rangle\) of order \(7\). Let \(H=\langle a\rangle\) be a Sylow \(3\)-subgroup. Since \(N\cap H=\{e\}\) and \(|N||H|=21\), we have \(G=NH\).

Normality of \(N\) gives
\[
aba^{-1}=b^r
\]
for some \(r\in\{1,\ldots,6\}\). Because \(a^3=e\), conjugating three times gives \(b=b^{r^3}\), hence \(r^3\equiv1\pmod 7\). The solutions are \(r\equiv1,2,4\pmod 7\). If \(r=1\), then \(a\) and \(b\) commute, and because they generate \(G\), the group would be abelian. Thus \(r=2\) or \(r=4\). If \(r=4\), replace \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\); the induced automorphism is then the inverse of exponentiation by \(4\), namely exponentiation by \(2\) modulo \(7\). Therefore generators may be chosen so that
\[
a^3=b^7=e,\qquad aba^{-1}=b^2.
\]

Applying the same argument to \(G'\), choose generators \(c,d\) such that
\[
c^3=d^7=e,\qquad cdc^{-1}=d^2.
\]

Every element of \(G\) has a unique expression \(b^j a^i\), where \(0\le j<7\) and \(0\le i<3\). Indeed, existence follows from \(G=NH\), and uniqueness follows from \(N\cap H=\{e\}\). Likewise, every element of \(G'\) has a unique expression \(d^j c^i\).

Define
\[
\Phi:G\to G',\qquad \Phi(b^j a^i)=d^j c^i.
\]
This is well-defined and bijective by uniqueness of the normal forms. Moreover,
\[
(b^j a^i)(b^\ell a^k)=b^{j+2^i\ell}a^{i+k},
\]
with exponents reduced modulo \(7\) and \(3\), respectively. The identical relation in \(G'\) gives
\[
(d^j c^i)(d^\ell c^k)=d^{j+2^i\ell}c^{i+k}.
\]
Consequently \(\Phi(xy)=\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\) for all \(x,y\in G\). Thus \(\Phi\) is a bijective homomorphism, so \(G\cong G'\). Hence any two nonabelian groups of order \(21\) are isomorphic."}]}
